trial_name: STOP-IT — Trial of Short-Course Antimicrobial Therapy for Intraabdominal Infection (2015)
citation: Sawyer RG, Claridge JA, Nathens AB, et al. Trial of Short-Course Antimicrobial Therapy for Intraabdominal Infection. N Engl J Med. 2015;372(21):1996-2005
one_liner: In adults with complicated intra-abdominal infection and adequate source control, a fixed 4-day antimicrobial course achieved similar 30-day outcomes to longer therapy guided by resolution of physiological abnormalities.

pico.population: Adults (>=16 years) with complicated intra-abdominal infection with adequate source control and post-procedure fever, leukocytosis, or gut dysfunction.
pico.intervention: Fixed short-course antimicrobials stopped within 24 hours of day 4 (total 3-4 days).
pico.comparison: Physiology-guided antimicrobials continued until 2 days after resolution of fever, leukocytosis, and GI dysfunction (max 10 days).
pico.outcome: Composite of surgical-site infection, recurrent intra-abdominal infection, or death within 30 days.

background.existing_knowledge: Complicated intra-abdominal infections (cIAI) were traditionally treated with broad-spectrum antimicrobials until resolution of fever, leukocytosis, and ileus.
background.knowledge_gap: Whether continuing antibiotics until physiological resolution improves patient outcomes or merely increases antimicrobial exposure remained unproven in randomised trials.
background.hypothesis: Fixed short-course antimicrobial therapy (4 days) after adequate source control yields similar 30-day clinical outcomes compared to continuing therapy until physiological recovery.

methods.design: Randomised, multicentre, investigator-initiated, pragmatic, open-label clinical trial with central allocation stratified by enrolling site and appendiceal vs non-appendiceal source.
methods.setting: Hospital-based surgical and percutaneous source-control pathways across multiple centres.

inclusion: Complicated intra-abdominal infection requiring hospitalisation and open, laparoscopic, or percutaneous source control
Within 24 hours post-intervention had WBC >11,000/mm3, temperature >=38.0°C, or GI dysfunction preventing normal diet
Adequate source control achieved as determined by local investigator and principal investigator
exclusion: Inability to obtain consent or inadequate source control
High likelihood of death within 72 hours or planned relaparotomy
Perforated gastric/duodenal ulcer treated within 24 hours of symptom onset
Traumatic bowel injury treated within 12 hours
Gangrenous appendicitis or peritonitis without confirmatory/positive cultures
Ischaemic or necrotic intestine without perforation and without positive cultures
Primary spontaneous bacterial peritonitis or CAPD catheter-related infection
Primary skin closure of an open incision in diffuse peritonitis (open abdomen)
Pregnancy or concurrent infection requiring >4 days of therapy

methods.intervention: Fixed short-course arm: Antimicrobials stopped within 24 hours after assignment to day 4 strategy (operationalised as 3–4 full days total); drug choice at treating team discretion.
methods.comparison: Physiological-resolution arm: Antimicrobials continued until 2 ± 1 days after resolution of leukocytosis (WBC <=11,000/mm3), fever (<38.0°C), and GI dysfunction adequate for enteral nutrition (maximum 10 days).
methods.sample_size_power: Protocol planned 1,120 patients to detect a 10% absolute difference in the primary composite outcome with 80% power at alpha=0.05. Enrolled 518 patients (517 analysed ITT).
methods.primary_outcome: Composite of surgical-site infection, recurrent intra-abdominal infection, or death within 30 days of the index procedure.
secondary_outcomes: Time to diagnosis of SSI and recurrent infection

headline_bullets: Primary composite outcome was identical between short-course (~4 days) and control arms (21.8% vs 22.3%, P=0.92).
Clear exposure separation was achieved with a 4-day median reduction in antimicrobial duration (4.0 vs 8.0 days, P<0.001).
Diagnosis of intra-abdominal complications occurred significantly later in the control arm, consistent with antibiotic suppression rather than prevention.

outcomes_table.outcome: Primary composite (SSI, recurrent intra-abdominal infection, or death by 30 days)
outcomes_table.note: No difference observed between 4-day and physiology-guided therapy.
Low overall mortality limited power for death endpoint.
Significant separation of experimental exposure variable.
Numerically higher in fixed-duration arm; non-significant.
No difference in hospital length of stay metrics.

safety: Extra-abdominal infection occurred in 8.9% (23/257) of short-course vs 5.0% (13/260) of control patients (P=0.11).
Clostridioides difficile infection occurred in 1.9% (5/257) vs 1.2% (3/260) (P=0.71).

domains.notes: Centralised randomisation stratified by site and appendiceal vs non-appendiceal source preserved balance.
Unblinded open-label design allowed potential threshold bias for secondary diagnostic testing.
518 randomised with 517 analysed at 30 days (99.8% follow-up).
Protocol-adherent antimicrobial duration was 81.8% in short-course vs 72.7% in control.
Balanced baseline severity (APACHE II 9.9 ± 3.9 vs 10.3 ± 4.0; healthcare-associated infection 36.8% vs 36.2%; percutaneous drainage 32.6% vs 33.1%; colon/rectal source 34.1% vs 31.5%).

internal_validity.verdict: Internal validity is moderate due to open-label design, lower enrolment than protocol power target, and incomplete protocol adherence.

domains.notes: Representative of adult hospitalised surgical patients receiving timely source control for cIAI.
Applicable in centers capable of effective source control; non-applicable to open abdomen or unmanaged source control.

external_validity.verdict: External validity is good for stable adults with cIAI who have achieved effective source control, but limited for uncontained sepsis or open abdomen.

strengths: Pragmatic multicentre RCT targeting a key real-world stewardship decision point
Excellent follow-up rate (99.8% primary outcome ascertainment)
Clear separation in treatment exposure (median 4 vs 8 days)
limitations: Open-label design may influence clinical diagnostic thresholds
Sample size (518) was under half the protocol target of 1,120
Source control adequacy was investigator-judged without explicit standardized criteria

critical_appraisal.summary: A high-impact pragmatic trial demonstrating that extending antibiotics beyond source control based on persistent physiological signs provides no clinical benefit, though underpowered for formal equivalence.
strengths: Focus on clinically important composite endpoints
weaknesses: Suboptimal protocol adherence in control group

sections.authors_conclusion: In patients with complicated intra-abdominal infection who underwent adequate source control, the outcomes after fixed short-course antimicrobial therapy (~4 days) were similar to those after a course guided by resolution of physiological abnormalities.

clinical_bottom_line.verdict: Stop antimicrobials at day 4 after effective source control for cIAI; do not routinely prolong treatment for isolated persistent physiological abnormalities.
clinical_bottom_line.applies_to: Adult patients with complicated intra-abdominal infection who have achieved successful surgical or percutaneous source control.
clinical_bottom_line.does_not_mean: Does not mean 4 days is sufficient if source control is incomplete, or in patients with pancreatitis or open abdomens.
implementation_caveats: Source control must be confirmed adequate prior to stopping antimicrobials
Persistent fever or leukocytosis beyond day 4 should trigger re-evaluation for source failure rather than routine antibiotic continuation

controversies.notes: Enrolled 518 of planned 1,120 target patients; shows similar point estimates but lacks power to declare strict statistical non-inferiority.
Demonstrates that definitive source control dominates outcome, while extra antibiotic days mostly suppress delayed diagnostic recognition of complications.

unresolved_questions: Optimal antibiotic duration in patients with borderline or incomplete initial source control
Safety of fixed short-course strategies in severely immunocompromised hosts

quick_recall.one_line_takeaway: After adequate source control for intra-abdominal infection, stop antibiotics at 4 days; continuing antibiotics for persistent fever or leukocytosis delays diagnosis of failure without improving outcomes.
